Siddique Ahmed Chowdhury with AT Chowdhury, Shafiqur Rahman, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner. 
Muhammad Habibur Rahman, Advocate ----- For the Opposite Party No.1.

Yar Ali Khan Chowdhury ----- Petitioner.
Vs.

full_judgment:
This petition under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is directed against an order dated 20.3.69 passed in Misc. Case No. 262/66 by Mr. M Islam, Dist. Judge Chittagong rejecting the prayer of the petitioner. Yar Ali Khan Chowdhury for examination of two witnesses namely, one Mr. Anwar Ali Chowdhury and one Mr. OR Nizam (who is since reported to be dead) on commission and issuing notice under Order 12, rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure for admission of certain documents. 

 2. The facts relating to the present petition in brief are that on 14.12.66 the petitioner. filed an application under section 50 read with section 35(1) of the East Pakistan Waqfs Ordinance 1962 (which will hereinafter be referred to as (the Ordinance) challenging the validity of an order dated 15.9.66 passed in Misc. Case No. 4/40 by Mr. N I Khan, Administrator of Waqfs, East Pakistan directing the petitioner. 

 As against the direction contained in clause (b) above the petitioner filed an application under Article 98 of the Constitution being petition No. 604 of 66 and the direction of the Administrator of Waqf for payment of Rs. 70,433.33 paisa was cancelled and as against the direction contained in clause (c) above namely, directing the petitioner to vacate the house in Chandanpura which was based upon the finding that the property at Chandanpura was Waqf property, the petitioner filed an application under section 50 read with sec. 35(1) of the Ordinance before the Dist. Judge of Chittagong which was registered as Misc. Case No. 262 of 1966. The application was duly admitted by the District Judge on 14.12.66 the operation of the impugned order of the Administrator of Waqf was stayed. Notices were issued and the case proceeded. Opposite party No. 1 Mokbul Ahmed Chowdhury and opposite party No. 5 and Ali Chowdhury entered appearance and filed written statements. On 15.3.69 the petitioner filed two applications in one of which he prayed for examining two witnesses on commission and in the other he prayed for directing the contesting OPs to admit certain documents under order 12. rule 4 CPC. By his Order dated 20.3.69 the learned District Judge rejected both the petitions and against the said order the petitioner obtained this rule. 

 "The learned lawyer appearing on behalf of the OP argued for rejecting those two applications. He has submitted that the present Misc. case is an appeal against the order of the Waqf Administrator and as such there is no scope of taking evidence or for issuing notice under Order 12 rule 4 CPC. The Waqf Administrator alone is authorized to decide whether any particular property is Waqf property or not. If any party is aggrieved by the order of the Waqf Administrator it may submit a petition to the District Judge the District Judge is only to see if the order in question of the Waqf Administrator is competent and in conformity with law and nothing beyond that. So there is no scope for any evidence in this court nor there is any necessity for admission of facts. I am inclined to agree with him on all these points. 

 6. Mr. Siddique Ahmed Chowdhury appearing on behalf of the petitioner challenges the legality and propriety of the aforesaid order on the ground that the learned District Judge misconstrued the provision of section 50 read with section 35(1) of the Ordinance and fell into an error by treating the application before him to be an appeal. He has  further contended that since the petitioner challenged the order of the Administrator declaring the entire Chandanpura property to be Waqf property and invoked the jurisdiction of the District Judge for declaration as to whether that property (except l/6th share thereof) was Waqf property or not, the petition for all intents and purposes should have been treated as suit for the purpose of determination of the question and the learned District Judge had no jurisdiction to debar the petitioner from adducing evidences and taking steps according to the provision of Order 12 rule 4 CPC which is applicable in the trial of civil suit. Mr. Muhammad Habibur Rahman appearing on behalf of the opposite party No. 1 contended that the Ordinance gives the District Judge judicial control over the work of the Administrator and in the exercise of his function the District Judge is competent to reject the prayer for examination of witnesses on production of any document if, he considers that the prayer was made for the purpose of vexation and delay and in this connection he referred to the provision of sub-section (2) section 35 of the Ordinance. 

 7. It appears that the District Judge rejected the prayer of the petitioner upon observation that the Misc. case before him was an appeal against the order of the Waqf Administrator and as such there was no scope of taking evidence or issuing notice under Order 12 rule 4 CPC. The question therefore arises does the District Judge function as a court of appeal when he exercises jurisdiction under section 50 read with sub-section (1) of section 35 of the Ordinance. 

 10. There, are two other sections in the Ordinance vide sections 40 and 43 wherein reference has been made about the District Judge, Under sub-section (1) of section 40 a mutwalli may apply to the Administrator for his opinion advice or direction on any question affecting the management or administration of the Waqf property or On any point in a deed of Waqf requiring clarification and if the Administrator cannot suitably dispose of the question he may refer the mutwalli to the court of the District Judge and if the mutwalli applies by petition to such court, the court shall give its opinion, advice and direction in the manner provided in sub-sections 2 and 3. Section 43 lays down that in the case of any Waqf of which there is no mutwalli or where there appears to the Administrator to be an impediment to the appointment of  mutwalli in terms of the deed of Waqf or where the successor to the office of Mutwalli is a minor, a person of unsound mind or a person adjudged insolvent by a competent court of law, the Administrator may for such period as he deems fit appoint a Person to act as mutwalli with notice to all the persons interested in the Waqf Any person aggrieved by such an appointment may within three months from the date of receipt of the notice, appeal to the District Judge and the decision of the District Judge shall be final. 

 11. An analysis of the aforesaid provisions of the Ordinance shows that an appeal lies to the District Judge only under sub-section 2 of section 32 and section 43. The jurisdiction of the District Judge in other matters namely those in sub-section (1) of section 35, sub-section 1 of section 40 and section 50 can be invoked only by a petition. The function of the District Judge under sub-section of section 40 is of an advisory nature, and naturally no right of appeal has been provided when he acts thereunder. When a petition is presented under section 50 challenging the decision of the Administrator that the particular property is a Waqf property as has been done in the instant case challenging the decision of the Administrator that the Chandanpura property is Waqf property, the petition is required to be disposed of in accordance with the provision of sub-section 1 of section 35 by a declaration by the District Judge himself as to whether the said property is Waqf property or not. Again when a petition is presented under sub-section 1 of section 35 challenging the validity of a notification issued under sub-section 1 of section 34 taking over and assuming the administration, control, management and maintenance of a Waqf property, such a petition is also required to be disposed of in the manner provided under that section by a similar declaration by the District Judge himself. A party aggrieved by a declaration so made by the District Judge in either case can file an appeal under sub-section 3 of section 35 to the High Court within sixty days of the order. 

 In dealing with such a petition he cannot refuse to fake oral or documentary evidence-on the ground that the District Judge is competent and in conformity with law and nothing beyond that. So there is no scope for any evidence in this court nor there is any necessity for admission of facts as was done in the instant case. The District Judge is of course empowered under sub-section 2 of section 35 of the Ordinance to refuse to issue any process for compelling-the attendance of any witness or the production of any document, if he considers that the prayer in this behalf has been made for the purpose of vexation and delay. 

 12. Mr. Muhammad Habibur Rahman invited my attention to the order sheet of the Misc case No. 262/66 to show that the petitioner had taken as many as 9 adjournments in the case and contended that it indicated that the petitions in question were filed for the purpose of vexation and delay and in view of the matter it cannot be said that the District Judge had no jurisdiction to pass the impugned order. Mr. Siddique Ahmed Chowdhury repelled this contention by pointing out that the contesting OPs did not object to the prayers for adjournments. It is unfortunate that the-case could not be disposed of due to frequent prayers for adjournments. Be that as it may if the District Judge in the present case rejected the two petitions in question finding, based upon, valid reasons, that they were filed for the purpose of vexation and delay, his order could not have been, assailed in law. The petitions were rejected on the grounds which are palpably untenable. 

 13. The result, therefore, is that the order dated 20.3.69 is set aside and the learned District Judge is directed to proceed with, the case in accordance with the law and in the light of the observation made above he should try to dispose of the case as expeditiously as possible. The Rule is accordingly made absolute without any order as to costs. The record of the case be sent back to the District Judge immediately.
